PACE (PROPERTY ASSESSED CLEAN ENERGY) FINANCING — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield · Alameda

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes, in general terms, California's statutory framework for Property Assessed Clean Energy ("PACE") financing: a voluntary contractual assessment that a property owner enters into with a public agency or its designated private program administrator to pay for renewable-energy, energy-efficiency, water-efficiency, or similar improvements permanently fixed to real property, primarily under Streets and Highways Code Chapter 29 (commencing with Section 5898.10) and the program-administrator provisions of Financial Code Sections 22680-22697. It concerns the property commonly known as 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield in Alameda County, California (Assessor's Parcel Number 123-456-789), owned by Pat Morgan, and financing under discussion, if any, with Sunrise PACE Program Administrator, Inc. for improvements described as: A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. This document does not itself create, approve, or record any assessment or lien; it does not calculate the specific cancellation deadline, financing amount, or eligibility outcome for any actual transaction; and it does not determine whether any actual PACE contract, disclosure, or program has complied with the requirements described here. It is meaningfully different from the corpus's existing California Solar Rights Act information sheet, which addresses an HOA's ability to restrict a member's *installation* of a solar system, not how that (or any other qualifying) improvement is *financed* through a property-tax-collected assessment.

WHAT A PACE ASSESSMENT IS
A PACE assessment is a form of voluntary contractual assessment authorized by Streets and Highways Code Chapter 29, under which a public agency finances qualifying improvements permanently fixed to real property and the property owner repays that financing as an assessment collected together with the property's regular tax bill, rather than as a conventional mortgage or home-improvement loan. The Legislature's stated intent for this chapter includes financing distributed generation renewable energy sources and energy or water efficiency improvements that are permanently affixed to the property, as well as certain other public improvements, described elsewhere in this chapter.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "It is also the intent of the Legislature that this chapter should be used to finance the installation or prepaid service contract, or both, of distributed generation renewable energy sources or energy efficiency improvements that are permanently fixed to residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, or other real property."
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.12(b), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.12(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.12.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the chapter's legislative-intent language in Section 5898.12(b), which states the Legislature's purpose in enacting the chapter; it is not itself an operative rule establishing an individual owner's rights or obligations, and it does not address the chapter's separate public-improvement or water-efficiency-only financing purposes described in Section 5898.12(c)-(d), which this document does not cover. A CourtListener search for on-topic California case law (query: "PACE assessment Property Assessed Clean Energy California contractual assessment lien") returned results rather than a rate-limit error, including a currently pending California Supreme Court matter, Morgan v. Ygrene Energy Fund, Inc., S277628 (argued from the Fourth Appellate District, opinion filed by the Court of Appeal Nov. 1, 2022 and Nov. 21, 2022, Supreme Court docket entry Dec. 4, 2025); this document nonetheless relies only on the statutory text itself, because verifying an exact contiguous quotation from a PDF-formatted judicial opinion was outside the scope of the leginfo-webpage-based double-fetch method used to verify every citation in this document, and because that litigation's outcome was not established as final at the time this sheet was checked.

THE ASSESSMENT IS A VOLUNTARY CONTRACT, NOT A GOVERNMENT MANDATE
A PACE assessment program exists only where a public agency's legislative body has designated an area and adopted a resolution making the financing available, and within that area, participation by any individual property owner is a matter of the owner's own voluntary contractual assessment with the public agency (or its program administrator) — not an assessment the public agency imposes on the owner without the owner's agreement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The legislative body of any public agency may also determine that it would be convenient, advantageous, and in the public interest to designate an area within the public agency, which may encompass the entire public agency or a lesser portion, within which authorized public agency officials and property owners may enter into voluntary contractual assessments to finance the installation of distributed generation renewable energy sources or energy or water efficiency improvements that are permanently fixed to real property pursuant to this chapter."
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.20(a)(2), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.20(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.20.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Section 5898.20(a)(2), the provision authorizing the renewable-energy/efficiency-improvement branch of the program; it does not quote the separate, older public-improvement branch in Section 5898.20(a)(1), which this document does not otherwise cover, and it does not describe the resolution-of-intention and public-hearing process (Sections 5898.20(b), 5898.22, 5898.24) by which a public agency establishes such a program in the first place, which is a public-agency-side procedural matter distinct from an individual owner's contract.

THE ASSESSMENT BECOMES A LIEN COLLECTED WITH THE PROPERTY TAX BILL
Once levied, a PACE assessment, together with any interest and penalties on it, becomes a lien against the property that continues until paid, and the assessment is collected in the same manner and at the same time as the general property taxes on the property, subject to the same delinquency and default remedies, unless a different collection procedure is separately authorized.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Assessments levied pursuant to this chapter, and the interest and any penalties thereon shall constitute a lien against the lots and parcels of land on which they are made, until they are paid."
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.30 (first sentence), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.30 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.30.)
  "Division 10 (commencing with Section 8500), insofar as those provisions are not in conflict with this chapter, Article 13 (commencing with Section 53930) of, and Article 13.5 (commencing with Section 53938) of, Chapter 4 of Part 1 of Division 2 of Title 5 of the Government Code apply to the imposition and collection of assessments contracted for pursuant to this chapter, including, but not limited to, provisions related to lien priority, the collection of assessments in the same manner and at the same time as the general taxes of the city or county on real property, unless another procedure has been authorized by the legislative body or by statute, and any penalties and remedies in the event of delinquency and default."
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.30 (second sentence), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.30 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.30.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the two operative sentences of Section 5898.30; it does not itself resolve, and the statute's text alone does not state, the relative lien priority between a PACE assessment and a first mortgage or deed of trust recorded before the assessment in every circumstance — that question is addressed by cross-referenced Government Code lien-priority provisions this document does not quote, and has also been the subject of litigation (see the CourtListener disclosure in the companion 'What a PACE Assessment Is' clause above) that this document does not resolve.

THE STATUTORY 5% CAP ON COMBINED ANNUAL TAXES AND ASSESSMENTS
A public agency may not allow a property owner to participate in a PACE program if doing so would make the property's total annual property taxes and assessments exceed 5 percent of the property's market value, measured at the time the owner's contractual assessment is approved. This cap does not, however, excuse the owner from the contract once entered: the statute expressly provides that the owner's contractual obligations are not voided or released even if the 5% figure is later exceeded after the contract is in place.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) A public agency shall not permit a property owner to participate in any program established pursuant to this chapter if the owner’s participation would result in the total amount of any annual property taxes and assessments exceeding 5 percent of the property’s market value, as determined at the time of approval of the owner’s contractual assessment."
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.15(a), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.15(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.15.)
  "Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to void or otherwise release a property owner from the contractual obligations incurred by a contractual assessment on a property, particularly in the event that the total amount of annual property taxes and assessments exceeds 5 percent of a property’s market value after the property owner has entered into a contractual assessment pursuant to this chapter."
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.15(b), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.15(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.15.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes both subsections (a) and (b) of Section 5898.15; it does not describe how 'market value' for purposes of this specific cap is determined (the statute does not, in this section, specify a required valuation method for the cap itself, in contrast to the separate value-representation restriction in Section 5898.17(c) addressed in a companion clause), and it does not address the parallel, differently-worded 5% test that applies specifically to the residential-four-units-or-fewer right-to-cancel program under Section 5898.16(a)(1), which this document does not separately quote.

THE STATUTORY RIGHT TO CANCEL — THREE BUSINESS DAYS, FIVE FOR SENIOR CITIZENS
For a PACE contractual assessment on residential property with four or fewer units, the property owner has a statutory right to cancel without cost, running through the third business day after the latest of: the date the owner signed the contractual assessment, the date the owner received the Financing Estimate and Disclosure, or the date the owner received the notice of the right to cancel. For a property owner who is a senior citizen, this deadline is extended: every reference to the third or third business day in the statutory cancellation document is changed to the fifth business day instead. A 'senior citizen' for this purpose is an individual who is 65 years of age or older.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "You may cancel this transaction, without cost, on or before midnight on the third business day after whichever of the following events occurs last:"
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.16(b)(1)(A), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.16(b)(1)(A) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.16.)
  "References to “third” in the notice to cancel document set forth in subparagraph (A) shall be changed to “fifth” for a property owner who is a senior citizen."
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.16(b)(1)(B), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.16(b)(1)(B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.16.)
  "“Senior citizen” means an individual who is 65 years of age or older."
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.16(d)(2), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.16(d)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.16.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the statutory Right to Cancel document text set out in Section 5898.16(b)(1)(A)-(B) and the senior-citizen definition in Section 5898.16(d)(2); it does not calculate an actual cancellation deadline for any specific transaction, which depends on identifying the latest of the three triggering events for that transaction and counting business days from it. It also does not cover the separate mechanics of how a cancellation notice is deemed given (Section 5898.16(b)(2)) or the program administrator's own 20-calendar-day obligation to discharge the lien and refund money after a valid cancellation, both of which this document does not quote. Section 5898.16 is itself scheduled to be repealed and replaced by a differently-numbered successor version of the same section effective January 1, 2029; this clause reflects the version of Section 5898.16 in effect as of the date checked above, not the version that becomes operative on that later date.

THE REQUIRED FINANCING ESTIMATE AND DISCLOSURE
Before a residential property owner (four or fewer units) may consummate a PACE contractual assessment, the statutorily prescribed Financing Estimate and Disclosure — or a substantially equivalent document displaying the same information in a substantially similar format — must be completed and delivered to the owner. That disclosure must be given as a printed paper copy in type no smaller than 12 points, unless the owner affirmatively opts out of the paper copy in writing by signing a printed paper document, in which case an electronic copy is provided instead.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) The disclosure set forth below, or a substantially equivalent document that displays the same information in a substantially similar format, shall be completed and delivered to a property owner before the property owner consummates a voluntary contractual assessment described in this chapter for purposes specified in paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 5898.20 or Section 5899, 5899.3, or 5899.4, or a special tax described in Section 53328.1 of the Government Code."
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.17(a), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.17(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.17.)
  "The disclosure shall be provided to the property owner as a printed paper copy in no smaller than 12-point type, unless the property owner opts out of receiving a printed paper copy in writing by signing a printed paper document."
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.17(a) (format requirement), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.17(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.17.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the threshold delivery-and-format requirement in Section 5898.17(a); the disclosure form itself is a lengthy, multi-part document (cost breakdown, APR, prepayment terms, and the acknowledgment items quoted in the companion 'statutory penalty' and 'sale or refinance' clauses below) that this document does not reproduce in full. This requirement, by its own terms in Section 5898.17(b)(1), applies only to residential property with four or fewer units; commercial, industrial, or agricultural PACE financing is not covered by this document. The leginfo URL cited here resolves to a version-picker rather than to statutory text: two versions of Section 5898.17 are on file (one amended as amended by Stats. 2018, Ch. 837, Sec. 10, the other as added by Sec. 11 of the same chapter, each amended by Stats. 2020, Ch. 158), and leginfo disambiguates them only through a form submission, not through a link. Both quotes in this clause were confirmed verbatim against the version amended by Stats. 2020, Ch. 158, Sec. 13.5, which is the one carrying this language; the other version does not contain it.

RESTRICTION ON REPRESENTATIONS THAT FINANCED IMPROVEMENTS WILL INCREASE PROPERTY VALUE
A public agency or other party to a PACE contractual assessment may not make any monetary or percentage representation to a property owner that the financed improvements will increase the property's value, unless that estimate is derived from an automated valuation model, a licensed real estate broker's price opinion, or an appraisal by a state-licensed real estate appraiser.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A public agency or other party to a voluntary contractual assessment described in this chapter for the purposes specified in paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 5898.20 or Section 5899, 5899.3, or 5899.4, or a special tax described in Section 53328.1 of the Government Code shall not make any monetary or percentage representations of increased value to a property owner regarding the effect the financed improvements will have on the market value of the property unless that public agency or other party derives its estimates of the market value using one of the following:"
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.17(c), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.17(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.17.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the opening restriction of Section 5898.17(c) and the introduction to its list of three permitted valuation-method categories; it does not reproduce the detailed sub-criteria the statute separately specifies for automated valuation models (found elsewhere in the program-administrator provisions), and it does not address representations about value that are not framed in monetary or percentage terms, which this section's plain text does not appear to reach.

REQUIRED DISCLOSURE OF LATE-PAYMENT PENALTIES
The statutory Financing Estimate and Disclosure form that must be delivered to a residential PACE applicant includes a required acknowledgment, initialed separately by the owner, that a late property tax payment carries a 10% penalty, late fees, and 1.5% per month interest, and that the property may become subject to foreclosure.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Statutory Penalties: If your property tax payment is late, the amount due will be subject to a 10% penalty, late fees, and 1.5% per month interest penalty as established by state law, and your property may be subject to foreclosure."
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.17(b)(1) (Financing Estimate and Disclosure form), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.17(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.17.)
  Known gap: This is the disclosure form's own summary language in Section 5898.17(b)(1); it states the general California property-tax delinquency penalty structure that applies once a PACE assessment is added to the tax bill, but this document does not separately verify or quote the underlying Revenue and Taxation Code provisions that actually set the 10% penalty and 1.5%-per-month rate, since the disclosure text itself, not those separate provisions, was this clause's chosen primary source.

REQUIRED DISCLOSURE THAT A SALE OR REFINANCE MAY REQUIRE PAYOFF
The same statutory disclosure form also requires the owner to separately acknowledge, in writing, that a mortgage lender refinancing the home may require payoff of the remaining PACE balance, and that if the home is sold, the buyer or the buyer's mortgage lender may likewise require the balance to be paid off as a condition of the sale.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "I understand that I may be required to pay off the remaining balance of this obligation by the mortgage lender refinancing my home. If I sell my home, the buyer or their mortgage lender may require me to pay off the balance of this obligation as a condition of sale."
  — Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.17(b)(1) (Financing Estimate and Disclosure form), Sts. & High. C. § 5898.17(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=SHC&sectionNum=5898.17.)
  Known gap: This is the disclosure form's own acknowledgment language in Section 5898.17(b)(1); it describes what a lender or buyer 'may' require rather than guaranteeing that outcome in every transaction, and the underlying legal basis for any such demand (for example, a lender's due-on-encumbrance or underwriting policy) arises from the separate mortgage contract or the buyer's own financing terms, not from this statute, which this document does not address.

PROGRAM ADMINISTRATOR PREREQUISITES BEFORE EXECUTING A RESIDENTIAL ASSESSMENT CONTRACT
Separately from the disclosure and cancellation requirements above, California's PACE program administrator statute bars a program administrator from executing an assessment contract — and bars commencement of the underlying home improvement work — unless a defined list of eligibility criteria is satisfied, including that all property taxes on the property are current, with the administrator required to ask the owner whether there has been more than one late property-tax payment in the previous three years or since the current owner acquired the property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A program administrator shall not execute an assessment contract, and no work shall commence under a home improvement contract that is financed by that assessment contract nor shall that home improvement contract be executed unless the following criteria are satisfied:"
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22684 (introductory clause), Fin. C. § 22684 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22684.)
  "All property taxes for the property that will be subject to the assessment contract are current. The program administrator shall ask a property owner whether there has been no more than one late payment of property taxes on the property for the previous three years or since the current owner acquired the property, whichever period is shorter."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22684(a), Fin. C. § 22684(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22684.)
  Known gap: Financial Code Section 22684 lists fourteen lettered eligibility criteria, subsections (a) through (n); this clause quotes only the introductory bar and the property-tax-currency criterion in subsection (a). It does not quote the other twelve criteria (no large involuntary liens, no unrescinded notice of default, bankruptcy and mortgage-payment-history lookbacks, program geographic and measure eligibility, useful-life term limits, duplicate-assessment verification, no prepayment penalty, no reverse-mortgage properties, and a general verification-method mandate), which are addressed only in this gap note, not quoted as citations.

PROGRAM ADMINISTRATOR LIMITS ON THE AMOUNT FINANCED
Among the same eligibility criteria, the program administrator statute also caps the size of the financing itself: the assessment must be for less than 15% of the property's value on the first $700,000 of value (inclusive of existing assessments), and less than 10% of any remaining value above $700,000, and the combined total of PACE assessments plus mortgage-related debt on the property may not exceed 97% of the property's market value as established under the statute's separate valuation-methodology section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The financing is for less than 15 percent of the value of the property, up to the first seven hundred thousand dollars ($700,000) inclusive of the existing assessments, and is for less than 10 percent of the remaining value of the property above seven hundred thousand dollars ($700,000)."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22684(h), Fin. C. § 22684(h) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22684.)
  "The total PACE assessments and the mortgage-related debt on the property subject to the PACE assessment will not exceed 97 percent of the market value of the property as established by the valuation required by Section 22685."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22684(i), Fin. C. § 22684(i) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22684.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subsections (h) and (i) of Financial Code Section 22684 only; it does not quote or describe the separate valuation methodology required by Section 22685 (automated valuation models, broker price opinions, or appraisals, with detailed sub-criteria for each) that this 97% figure depends on, and it does not address what happens, beyond the general verification duty in subsection (k), if a property owner has an unrecorded PACE assessment the administrator was not told about.

THE PROGRAM ADMINISTRATOR'S ABILITY-TO-PAY DETERMINATION REQUIREMENT
Independent of the specific eligibility criteria above, the program administrator statute separately bars a program administrator from executing an assessment contract, or allowing the underlying home improvement work to begin, unless the administrator has made a reasonable, good-faith determination that the property owner has a reasonable ability to pay the annual payment obligations the PACE assessment will create.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A program administrator shall not execute an assessment contract, and no work shall commence under a home improvement contract that is financed by that assessment contract nor shall that home improvement contract be executed unless the program administrator makes a reasonable good faith determination that the property owner has a reasonable ability to pay the annual payment obligations for the PACE assessment."
  — Cal. Fin. Code § 22686, Fin. C. § 22686 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FIN&sectionNum=22686.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only Section 22686's general 'reasonable good faith determination' standard; it does not quote the more detailed income/asset/debt-obligation factors and documentation process set out in the separate Financial Code Section 22687, which this document does not reproduce, so the specific method by which any given administrator must reach that determination is not addressed here.

I understand that this document is informational only: it does not itself create, approve, cancel, or record any assessment or lien; it does not calculate any actual cancellation deadline, financing amount, or eligibility outcome; and it does not determine whether any actual PACE contract, disclosure, or program has complied with the requirements this sheet describes.

expectedJSON.body: A public agency may not allow a property owner to participate in a PACE program if doing so would make the property's total annual property taxes and assessments exceed 5 percent of the property's market value, measured at the time the owner's contractual assessment is approved. This cap does not, however, excuse the owner from the contract once entered: the statute expressly provides that the owner's contractual obligations are not voided or released even if the 5% figure is later exceeded after the contract is in place.

citations.quote: (a) A public agency shall not permit a property owner to participate in any program established pursuant to this chapter if the owner’s participation would result in the total amount of any annual property taxes and assessments exceeding 5 percent of the property’s market value, as determined at the time of approval of the owner’s contractual assessment.

Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to void or otherwise release a property owner from the contractual obligations incurred by a contractual assessment on a property, particularly in the event that the total amount of annual property taxes and assessments exceeds 5 percent of a property’s market value after the property owner has entered into a contractual assessment pursuant to this chapter.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes both subsections (a) and (b) of Section 5898.15; it does not describe how 'market value' for purposes of this specific cap is determined (the statute does not, in this section, specify a required valuation method for the cap itself, in contrast to the separate value-representation restriction in Section 5898.17(c) addressed in a companion clause), and it does not address the parallel, differently-worded 5% test that applies specifically to the residential-four-units-or-fewer right-to-cancel program under Section 5898.16(a)(1), which this document does not separately quote.

expectedJSON.body: For a PACE contractual assessment on residential property with four or fewer units, the property owner has a statutory right to cancel without cost, running through the third business day after the latest of: the date the owner signed the contractual assessment, the date the owner received the Financing Estimate and Disclosure, or the date the owner received the notice of the right to cancel. For a property owner who is a senior citizen, this deadline is extended: every reference to the third or third business day in the statutory cancellation document is changed to the fifth business day instead. A 'senior citizen' for this purpose is an individual who is 65 years of age or older.

citations.quote: You may cancel this transaction, without cost, on or before midnight on the third business day after whichever of the following events occurs last:
References to “third” in the notice to cancel document set forth in subparagraph (A) shall be changed to “fifth” for a property owner who is a senior citizen.
“Senior citizen” means an individual who is 65 years of age or older.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes the statutory Right to Cancel document text set out in Section 5898.16(b)(1)(A)-(B) and the senior-citizen definition in Section 5898.16(d)(2); it does not calculate an actual cancellation deadline for any specific transaction, which depends on identifying the latest of the three triggering events for that transaction and counting business days from it. It also does not cover the separate mechanics of how a cancellation notice is deemed given (Section 5898.16(b)(2)) or the program administrator's own 20-calendar-day obligation to discharge the lien and refund money after a valid cancellation, both of which this document does not quote. Section 5898.16 is itself scheduled to be repealed and replaced by a differently-numbered successor version of the same section effective January 1, 2029; this clause reflects the version of Section 5898.16 in effect as of the date checked above, not the version that becomes operative on that later date.

That disclosure must be given as a printed paper copy in type no smaller than 12 points, unless the owner affirmatively opts out of the paper copy in writing by signing a printed paper document, in which case an electronic copy is provided instead.

citations.quote: (a) The disclosure set forth below, or a substantially equivalent document that displays the same information in a substantially similar format, shall be completed and delivered to a property owner before the property owner consummates a voluntary contractual assessment described in this chapter for purposes specified in paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 5898.20 or Section 5899, 5899.3, or 5899.4, or a special tax described in Section 53328.1 of the Government Code.

The disclosure shall be provided to the property owner as a printed paper copy in no smaller than 12-point type, unless the property owner opts out of receiving a printed paper copy in writing by signing a printed paper document.

This requirement, by its own terms in Section 5898.17(b)(1), applies only to residential property with four or fewer units; commercial, industrial, or agricultural PACE financing is not covered by this document. The leginfo URL cited here resolves to a version-picker rather than to statutory text: two versions of Section 5898.17 are on file (one amended as amended by Stats. 2018, Ch. 837, Sec. 10, the other as added by Sec. 11 of the same chapter, each amended by Stats. 2020, Ch. 158), and leginfo disambiguates them only through a form submission, not through a link. Both quotes in this clause were confirmed verbatim against the version amended by Stats. 2020, Ch. 158, Sec. 13.5, which is the one carrying this language; the other version does not contain it.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from the disclosure and cancellation requirements above, California's PACE program administrator statute bars a program administrator from executing an assessment contract — and bars commencement of the underlying home improvement work — unless a defined list of eligibility criteria is satisfied, including that all property taxes on the property are current, with the administrator required to ask the owner whether there has been more than one late property-tax payment in the previous three years or since the current owner acquired the property.

citations.quote: A program administrator shall not execute an assessment contract, and no work shall commence under a home improvement contract that is financed by that assessment contract nor shall that home improvement contract be executed unless the following criteria are satisfied:

All property taxes for the property that will be subject to the assessment contract are current. The program administrator shall ask a property owner whether there has been no more than one late payment of property taxes on the property for the previous three years or since the current owner acquired the property, whichever period is shorter.

The total PACE assessments and the mortgage-related debt on the property subject to the PACE assessment will not exceed 97 percent of the market value of the property as established by the valuation required by Section 22685.

citations.quote: A program administrator shall not execute an assessment contract, and no work shall commence under a home improvement contract that is financed by that assessment contract nor shall that home improvement contract be executed unless the program administrator makes a reasonable good faith determination that the property owner has a reasonable ability to pay the annual payment obligations for the PACE assessment.
